### Tutorial 7.3: Evaluating Three Pricing Strategies with Scenario Manager

**Context and objective.** You will define three pricing scenarios for the Beacon dining table and use Scenario Manager to compare their effects on break-even volume, profit, and contribution margin. This exercise simulates the kind of analysis a product manager would request before a pricing decision.

**Prerequisites.** Complete Tutorial 7.2. Your CVP_DiningTable worksheet should have the assumption cells in B4 (Selling Price), B5 (Variable Cost), and B6 (Fixed Costs), along with the break-even calculation in B11 and the profit calculation at a reference volume.

**Step 1.** Before creating scenarios, identify a reference volume to use for comparing profit across scenarios. In cell A33, type "Reference Volume for Comparison" and in cell B33, enter 500. In cell A34, type "Profit at Reference Volume" and in cell B34, enter the formula =(B33*$B$4) - (B33*$B$5) - $B$6. This calculates the profit at 500 units sold under the current assumptions.

**Step 2.** Go to the Data tab, click "What-If Analysis," and select "Scenario Manager." Click "Add." Name the first scenario "Base Case." In the Changing Cells box, enter B4,B5,B6 (the three assumption cells). Click OK. In the Scenario Values dialog, enter the current values: B4 = 1850, B5 = 1040, B6 = 245000. Click Add to continue to the next scenario.

**Step 3.** Name the second scenario "Premium Strategy." This scenario increases the selling price by 10% and increases fixed costs by $35,000 to cover additional marketing. Enter B4 = 2035 (1850 times 1.10, rounded), B5 = 1040 (unchanged), B6 = 280000. Click Add.

**Step 4.** Name the third scenario "Volume Strategy." This scenario decreases the selling price by 8% to gain market share, while keeping costs unchanged. Enter B4 = 1702 (1850 times 0.92, rounded), B5 = 1040, B6 = 245000. Click OK.

**Step 5.** In the Scenario Manager dialog, you should now see three scenarios listed. Click "Summary." In the Result Cells box, enter B7,B8,B11,B34 (contribution margin per unit, contribution margin ratio, break-even volume, and profit at reference volume). Select "Scenario Summary" and click OK.

**Step 6.** Excel generates a Scenario Summary worksheet. Examine the results. The Base Case should show the values you calculated in Tutorial 7.2. The Premium Strategy should show a higher contribution margin per unit, a lower break-even volume (because the per-unit margin rises faster than fixed costs), and a higher profit at the reference volume. The Volume Strategy should show a lower contribution margin per unit and a higher break-even volume, with lower profit at the reference volume.

Rows show the input values (Selling Price, Variable Cost, Fixed Costs) and output values (Contribution Margin per Unit, Contribution Margin Ratio, Break-Even Volume, Profit at 500 Units). *Figure 7.10: Scenario Summary worksheet generated by Scenario Manager. Three columns compare the Base Case, Premium Strategy, and Volume Strategy across input assumptions and key output measures for the Beacon dining table furniture line.*

| | Base Case | Premium Strategy | Volume Strategy |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Input Values** | | | |
| Selling Price per Unit | $1,850 | $2,035 | $1,702 |
| Variable Cost per Unit | $1,040 | $1,040 | $1,040 |
| Fixed Costs | $245,000 | $280,000 | $245,000 |
| **Output Values** | | | |
| Contribution Margin per Unit | $810 | $995 | $662 |
| Contribution Margin Ratio | 43.8% | 48.9% | 38.9% |
| Break-Even Volume (units) | 303 | 282 | 371 |
| Profit at 500 Units | $160,000 | $217,500 | $86,000 |

**Interpreting the scenarios.** The Premium Strategy generates the highest per-unit margin ($995) and the highest profit at 500 units ($217,500), and it achieves the lowest break-even volume (282 units) because the per-unit margin increase more than offsets the higher fixed costs. It depends, however, on the assumption that demand will not decline when the price increases. The Volume Strategy reduces the selling price to attract more customers, but its lower contribution margin means the company must sell 371 units just to break even, compared to 303 for the Base Case, and it produces the lowest profit at the reference volume. These trade-offs illustrate why scenario comparison is more informative than evaluating a single set of assumptions.

**Checkpoint.** Your workbook should now contain the Scenario Summary worksheet showing all three scenarios. The summary should make clear that the Premium Strategy produces the highest per-unit profit and the lowest break-even volume, while the Volume Strategy requires the highest sales volume to break even and produces the lowest profit at the reference volume. These trade-offs are exactly the kind of information the product management team needs for the pricing decision.
